findings.claim: The chronicler Alcuin wrote that 'never before has such terror appeared in Britain'
findings.truth: Alcuin was a scholar and letter-writer at Charlemagne's court, not a chronicler; the shock at Lindisfarne survives in his letters, not in a chronicle he wrote.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Alcuin' / 'Lindisfarne': Alcuin's account is a letter to King Aethelred of Northumbria.

findings.claim: By his death in 899 he was the only Anglo-Saxon king ever called 'the Great'.
findings.truth: Alfred was not called 'the Great' in his lifetime; the title was applied by much later writers. He is the only English king who carries it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Alfred the Great': the epithet dates from the sixteenth century onwards.

findings.claim: The peace negotiated with Guthrum, refined under Alfred's son Edward and his daughter Aethelflaed, formalised a division of the country.
findings.truth: Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed did not refine the treaty line: between 912 and 918 they conquered the Danelaw and pushed the frontier back.
findings.evidence: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle / Wikipedia 'Edward the Elder', 'Aethelflaed'.

findings.claim: units of land measurement (the wapentake, the carucate)
findings.truth: A carucate is a unit of land; a wapentake is a unit of local government, the Danelaw equivalent of a hundred.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Wapentake', 'Carucate'.

findings.claim: Comparison question labelled '4 marks - Two Ways Similar or Different'
findings.truth: On this paper the comparison question ('Explain two ways in which X and Y were similar/different') is worth 8 marks, not 4. Section A is four questions: source utility 8, significance 8, comparison 8, factors essay 16 plus 4 SPaG.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Paper 2 Section A question table; spec 2.2 (Section A four compulsory questions, 40 marks plus 4 SPaG).

findings.claim: One-word answers ('793.', '878.') and list answers ('Sky and they', '878 / Wessex / Guthrum')
findings.truth: House rules: a bare answer needs a fuller answer of a few words, and list answers fail the validator (one idea per card).
findings.evidence: house flashcard rules

findings.claim: Harald Hardrada of Norway (claiming through Cnut's son Magnus)
findings.truth: Magnus the Good was the son of Olaf II of Norway, not of Cnut. Hardrada's claim rested on the 1038 pact between Magnus and Cnut's son Harthacnut, by which the survivor would inherit the other's lands.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Harald Hardrada': claim based on the Magnus-Harthacnut agreement of 1038; Magnus was a son of Olaf Haraldsson.

findings.claim: For the 4-mark Two Ways Similar or Different question
findings.truth: The comparison question on this paper is worth 8 marks.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Paper 2 Section A question table.

findings.claim: North Sea Empire 'ruled from 1018-1028 onwards'
findings.truth: Cnut held England from 1016, Denmark from 1018 and Norway from 1028, until his death in 1035. The date range as written is meaningless.
findings.evidence: lesson content_html; Wikipedia 'Cnut the Great'.

findings.claim: Her unique position as queen of two rival dynasties commissioned the Encomium Emmae Reginae
findings.truth: A position cannot commission a book; Emma herself commissioned it. Left as written because the check brief excludes style.
findings.evidence: lesson text

findings.claim: In 1171 Henry took an army to Ireland and forced its high king and major lords to accept him as overlord.
findings.truth: Fifteen Irish kings and lords submitted in 1171, but the high king Ruaidri Ua Conchobair did not. He accepted Henry as overlord only under the Treaty of Windsor in 1175.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Norman invasion of Ireland': those who did not submit included Ruaidri, the high king; he swore fealty in 1175.

findings.claim: In 1204 the French king Philip Augustus invaded Normandy and overran it within months.
findings.truth: Philip's campaign ran from 1202; Chateau Gaillard fell in March 1204 and Rouen in June 1204.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Philip II of France', 'Loss of Normandy'.

findings.claim: All six questions are set as '8 marks - Explain a Development'.
findings.truth: This paper does not set an 'Explain a Development' question. Paper 2 Section A sets four: 'How useful is Source A' (8), 'Explain the significance of' (8), 'Explain two ways in which X and Y were similar/different' (8), and a factors essay (16 + 4 SPaG). Converted to the real forms with rebuilt mark schemes.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section A table; spec 4.4.1 shows the Paper 1 forms, which do not include it either.

findings.claim: Within a hundred years of Bordeaux's fall in 1453, English ships under John Hawkins ... and Walter Raleigh was promoting a colony at Roanoke
findings.truth: Hawkins sailed in 1562, 109 years after 1453, and Raleigh's Roanoke venture began in 1585, 132 years after.
findings.evidence: lesson 6 and lesson 7 content; Wikipedia 'John Hawkins', 'Roanoke Colony'.

findings.claim: the first European Jewish population to be formally banished by royal decree
findings.truth: England's 1290 expulsion was the first permanent, kingdom-wide expulsion. Earlier expulsions had happened elsewhere, including Philip Augustus's expulsion from the French royal lands in 1182, but Jews were allowed back after a few years.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Edict of Expulsion': the first time a European state permanently banned their presence; earlier local or temporary expulsions had taken place.

findings.claim: When the king defaulted on his debts in 1340, two of the great Florentine banking houses - the Bardi and Peruzzi - collapsed.
findings.truth: Edward III stopped paying around 1340, but the Peruzzi failed in 1343 and the Bardi in 1346.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Peruzzi', 'Compagnia dei Bardi'.

findings.claim: 'ready-made comparisons for the 4-mark question' (content) and 'For the 4-mark comparison question' (collapsible) and the same tariff in the exam tip and three mark schemes
findings.truth: The comparison question on this paper is worth 8 marks.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section A table.

findings.claim: Huguenots 'naturalised by Parliament in 1689' (also lesson 8 content, lesson 8 mark scheme and flashcard, lesson 11 mark scheme)
findings.truth: There was no 1689 naturalisation act for Huguenots. Parliament's general naturalisation act for foreign Protestants was passed on 23 March 1709 and repealed in 1711-12; before that, refugees relied on royal proclamations and individual denization.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Foreign Protestants Naturalization Act 1708': passed 23 March 1709, largely repealed 1711.

findings.claim: Comma-list answer 'Timber, wax, fur, pitch, tar and grain.' and bare answers '1290.', 'Usury.'
findings.truth: List answers fail the validator; bare answers need a few words of substance.
findings.evidence: house flashcard rules

findings.claim: Elizabeth I expelled the Hanseatic merchants from the Steelyard in 1597 (repeated in the key fact, conclusion, glossary, a knowledge check, a flashcard and two mark schemes)
findings.truth: The Emperor expelled the English Merchant Adventurers in 1597 and Elizabeth retaliated by suppressing the Steelyard in January 1598. Wikipedia gives 1598; many textbooks give 1597. Either change all nine places to 1598 or leave 1597 as the taught date - do not mix.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Steelyard': Queen Elizabeth suppressed the Steelyard and rescinded its privileges in 1598.
findings.ruling: Steelyard expulsion left at 1597 (textbook date); 1598 not worth a nine-field ripple.

findings.claim: By 1750 Britain held Barbados, Jamaica, the Leeward Islands, Antigua and St Kitts
findings.truth: Antigua and St Kitts are Leeward Islands, so the list treats them as separate colonies from a group they belong to.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Leeward Islands'.

findings.claim: The 1585 Roanoke expedition is described as the colony found empty in 1590.
findings.truth: There were two colonies. The 1585 settlers gave up and sailed home with Drake in 1586. A second group under John White landed in 1587, and it was that colony the 1590 relief mission found deserted.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Roanoke Colony'.

findings.claim: the 1630 'Great Migration' brought around 20,000 Puritans to Massachusetts under John Winthrop (repeated in the conclusion and a flashcard)
findings.truth: The Great Migration ran from 1630 to 1640 and brought about 20,000 settlers in total. Winthrop's fleet of 1630 carried around 700 passengers.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Puritan migration to New England (1620-1640)': about 20,000 over the period; the Winthrop Fleet delivered some 700 passengers.

findings.claim: Australia (claimed 1788, partly to dump convicts ...)
findings.truth: Cook claimed the east coast in 1770; 1788 is the date of the first convict settlement.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'History of Australia'.

findings.claim: 'Around _____ Pilgrims sailed on the Mayflower in 1620', answer 102
findings.truth: 102 was the number of passengers. The lesson itself says only about 35 of them were Separatists, so a student who has learned the lesson would pick 35 and be marked wrong.
findings.evidence: lesson content_html: 'Around 35 of the 102 passengers were Separatists'.

findings.claim: confiscated Catholic Irish land in six counties (Donegal, Tyrone, Tyrconnell, Armagh, Cavan and Fermanagh)
findings.truth: Tyrconnell is the Gaelic lordship that became County Donegal, so the list names it twice and omits Coleraine (later Londonderry). The six escheated counties were Armagh, Cavan, Coleraine, Donegal, Fermanagh and Tyrone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Plantation of Ulster': the six escheated counties were Donegal, Londonderry, Tyrone, Fermanagh, Cavan and Armagh.

findings.claim: land ... was redistributed to around 100,000 Lowland Scots and English Protestant settlers (1609)
findings.truth: About 12,000 adult planters were on plantation land by 1622 and around 20,000 adult male settlers by the 1630s (perhaps 80,000 people). The 100,000 figure belongs to the migration of 1650-1700.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Plantation of Ulster': 1622 survey c.12,000 adult planters; 1630s c.20,000 adult males; c.100,000 British settlers migrated 1650-1700.

findings.claim: 'Explain two ways in which religion shaped migration to and from Britain in the early modern period.' set as a comparison question
findings.truth: The comparison question compares two named events, developments, individuals or groups. This asks for two effects of one factor, which is not the form set. Reframed as a comparison of the Huguenot migration with the Ulster Plantation.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2: question 3 asks students to compare two key events, developments or the role of individuals or groups.

findings.claim: He showed a soldier's talent in skirmishes with the French at Arcot (1751) and Calcutta (1757)
findings.truth: Arcot was fought against the French, but Clive retook Calcutta from the Nawab of Bengal, not from the French.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Robert Clive': siege of Arcot 1751; recapture of Calcutta January 1757 from Siraj ud-Daulah.

findings.claim: Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) and finally Oudh (1856) all 'lapsed' to the Company (repeated in the key fact and a mark scheme)
findings.truth: Oudh was not annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. Dalhousie annexed it in 1856 on the ground of misgovernment; its ruler had heirs. This is a distinction examiners expect students to make.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Doctrine of lapse': Awadh is widely believed to have been annexed under the doctrine, but was in fact annexed under the pretext of mis-governance.

findings.claim: his impeachment trial (1788-95) prompted Pitt's India Act 1784
findings.truth: The India Act came first, in 1784. The trial began in 1788 and cannot have prompted an act passed four years earlier.
findings.evidence: lesson content_html: 'Pitt's India Act 1784 had already given Parliament a controlling Board'.

findings.claim: by 1888 controlled De Beers, which still mines most of the world's diamonds today
findings.truth: De Beers held as much as 90% of the market in the 1980s but supplies roughly a quarter of the world's diamonds today.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'De Beers': about 25% of global supply in 2021, down from as high as 90% in the 1980s.

findings.claim: prompted the 1904-05 Royal Commission on physical deterioration of British recruits
findings.truth: The body was the Inter-Departmental Committee on Physical Deterioration, which reported in 1904. It was not a Royal Commission. The lesson's own mark scheme names it correctly.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Inter-Departmental Committee on Physical Deterioration' (report 1904); lesson practice question 1.

findings.claim: This was bad biology - Darwin himself rejected the idea
findings.truth: Darwin did not campaign for social Darwinism, but the claim that he rejected it is a simplification; the phrase 'survival of the fittest' came from Herbert Spencer. Left as written.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Social Darwinism'

findings.claim: Two flashcards in the same lesson share the answer 'Around one million.'
findings.truth: Duplicate answers within a lesson fail the validator. The second card also repeats a figure that is wrong (see F36).
findings.evidence: house flashcard rules

findings.claim: The Great Famine ... pushed another one million to Britain (key fact, conclusion, mark scheme, flashcard)
findings.truth: About one million died and almost as many again emigrated, but most went on to North America. Britain received a large share through Liverpool rather than the whole million.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Irish migration to Great Britain': more than a million died and almost the same again emigrated, many passing through Liverpool and departing for the United States.

findings.claim: Cardinal Newman's 1851 conversion ... responded to this Irish-Catholic presence
findings.truth: John Henry Newman converted to Catholicism in 1845 and became a cardinal only in 1879, so there was no 1851 conversion and the title is anachronistic.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'John Henry Newman': received into the Catholic Church 9 October 1845; created cardinal 1879.

findings.claim: the political pressure that helped pass Catholic Emancipation (1829)
findings.truth: Catholic Emancipation was won in 1829 by O'Connell's Catholic Association in Ireland, sixteen years before famine migration. Crediting it to the Irish communities described in this paragraph inverts the sequence, and it belongs to a different option's content.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829'; spec AC part three lists Irish migration to Britain, not emancipation.

findings.claim: comparisons across vastly different periods are exactly what examiners want
findings.truth: An invented claim about examiner preference. The spec says only that the comparison question may target one part of the content or a combination of two.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2: 'The focus may target Part one, two, three or four or a combination of two parts'.

findings.claim: By 1945 Britain owed the United States the equivalent of around four years of national income (repeated in a mark scheme)
findings.truth: Britain's whole national debt, most of it owed at home, peaked at roughly two and a half times national income in 1946-47. The 1945 Anglo-American loan was $3.75 billion, a small fraction of a year's national income.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Anglo-American loan' and UK public debt series: debt peaked near 250% of GDP after 1945.

findings.claim: the Suez Canal - British- and French-owned since 1869
findings.truth: The canal company was French; Britain bought the Khedive's shares in 1875, six years after the canal opened.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Suez Canal Company': Britain purchased the Egyptian shareholding in 1875.

findings.claim: Examiners reward judgement, not balance for its own sake.
findings.truth: An invented claim about examiner preference. The spec says the essay requires a judgement and a sustained line of reasoning; it says nothing about rewarding judgement over balance.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, question 4 description.

findings.claim: The 1943 Bengal famine killed at least three million Indians; Churchill's government diverted food to British troops.
findings.truth: The death toll is right, but the mechanism is contested by historians. What is agreed is that the wartime government refused most requests to divert shipping for relief. Left as written; a rewrite would need a historiographical note.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Bengal famine of 1943'

findings.claim: The 1948 British Nationality Act, passed three weeks before the ship docked (also 'passed earlier that year' in the key fact, the revision tip and a mark scheme)
findings.truth: The Act received Royal Assent on 30 July 1948, five weeks AFTER Windrush docked on 22 June, and took effect on 1 January 1949. The passengers did not travel under it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'British Nationality Act 1948': Royal Assent 30 July 1948, commencement 1 January 1949.

findings.claim: the National Health Service (founded the same week Windrush docked)
findings.truth: The NHS opened on 5 July 1948, a fortnight after Windrush docked on 22 June. Lesson 14 makes the same error in reverse, saying the NHS opened three weeks before the ship docked.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'National Health Service': launched 5 July 1948.

findings.claim: In response to the Notting Hill attacks she founded the West Indian Gazette (1958) (repeated in a mark scheme)
findings.truth: The West Indian Gazette was launched in March 1958, four months BEFORE the Notting Hill attacks of August-September 1958. The carnival of January 1959 was the response to the attacks.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Claudia Jones': gazette founded March 1958; 'In August 1958, four months after the launch of WIG, the Notting Hill race riots occurred'.

findings.claim: supported the Stephen Lawrence-style legal organising that would mature in the 1970s
findings.truth: Stephen Lawrence was murdered in 1993, twenty-nine years after Claudia Jones died. The comparison is an anachronism inside a model answer.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Murder of Stephen Lawrence' (1993); Jones died December 1964.

findings.claim: Claudia Jones ... arrived in London via Trinidad
findings.truth: She was refused entry to Trinidad, her birthplace, and was then offered residence in Britain on humanitarian grounds.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Claudia Jones': offered residency in the United Kingdom after being refused entry to Trinidad and Tobago.

findings.claim: the largest single arrival of refugees since the Huguenots almost three centuries earlier (also in the key fact and a mark scheme)
findings.truth: Larger refugee movements came in between: around 250,000 Belgians in 1914, and the Polish resettlement after 1945, which lifted the Polish-born population of Britain from 44,642 in 1931 to 162,339 by the 1951 census.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Polish Resettlement Act 1947': citizenship offered to over 250,000 displaced Polish troops; 1951 census Polish-born 162,339.

findings.claim: The 2017 destruction of landing-card archives by the Home Office ... At least 164 people were wrongly removed
findings.truth: The landing cards were destroyed in 2010. The Home Office identified 164 cases of wrongful detention or removal, of which 83 were confirmed as wrongful deportations.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Windrush scandal': cards destroyed in 2010; by November 2018, 83 confirmed wrongful deportations with a further 81 feared.

findings.claim: The Attlee government built the welfare state out of these funds
findings.truth: Marshall aid eased the dollar shortage and the balance of payments; the welfare state was paid for out of taxation.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Marshall Plan'; UK public finance.

findings.claim: Macmillan applied for membership; Charles de Gaulle vetoed Britain's application twice (1963, 1967)
findings.truth: Macmillan made the 1961 application, vetoed in 1963. The second application, vetoed in 1967, was made by Harold Wilson.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'United Kingdom accession to the European Communities'.

findings.claim: By the 2011 census ... Polish-born residents were the largest non-UK-born group in Britain, and around one million Polish citizens settled between 2004 and 2014 (repeated in the key fact, conclusion, a mark scheme and a flashcard)
findings.truth: At the 2011 census India was the most common non-UK country of birth and Poland second; at the 2021-22 census India was still ahead (965,000 to 841,000). The Polish-born population passed one million only in the late 2010s.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Foreign-born population of the United Kingdom': 2021-22 census India 965,000, Poland 841,000; Poland-born 532,000 in 2010.

findings.claim: Polling consistently showed that immigration was the single most important issue for Leave voters (repeated in a mark scheme)
findings.truth: In Lord Ashcroft's post-referendum poll, 49% of Leave voters gave 'decisions about the UK should be taken in the UK' as their biggest single reason, and 33% gave control of immigration and borders. Sovereignty came first, immigration second.
findings.evidence: lordashcroftpolls.com, 'How the United Kingdom voted and why', 24 June 2016.

findings.claim: net migration ... 906,000 in the year to mid-2023 - nearly double the level under free movement
findings.truth: Net migration under free movement peaked at about 330,000 in the year to June 2016, so 906,000 is nearly three times that peak, not double.
findings.evidence: ONS long-term international migration series (net migration YE June 2016 c.336,000; YE June 2023 906,000).

findings.claim: Description is 104 characters
findings.truth: The house limit is under 100 characters.
findings.evidence: house validator limit

summary: 14 lessons checked. The exam framing was the biggest problem: 19 comparison questions carried a 4-mark tariff (the paper sets it at 8) and 20 questions were set in forms this paper does not use ('Explain a Development', 'Explain Effects'), all converted to the four real Section A forms with rebuilt mark schemes. Substantive errors fixed include Hardrada's claim through Magnus, the Ulster plantation counties, Oudh annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse, the British Nationality Act dated before Windrush, the West Indian Gazette dated after the Notting Hill attacks, Windrush landing cards destroyed in 2017, Britain owing the USA four years of national income, and Poland as the largest non-UK-born group in 2011.
